okr.objective: Corp Criadh is a Scottish ritual clay object used to work ill on others.
key_results: People in the Highlands used Corp Criadh until the 19th century.
Craftspeople stuck the doll with pins or cut it, then placed it in a stream so the water dissolved the clay.
The intended victim died when the doll dissolved, unless someone saw it first and broke the spell.
okr.evidence: Henderson, George. Survivals in Belief Among the Celts. Glasgow: James MacLeose and Sons, 1911, 16.

text: Corp Criadh, also called Corp Creagh, is a ritual object from Scottish tradition. Highlanders worked with such clay figures well into the 1800s. Users shaped a doll to hurt a neighbour or to take revenge on a disloyal lover. They pierced or sliced the model, then left it floating in a stream. Flowing water slowly wore the clay away. Once the figure dissolved altogether, the intended victim perished from those wounds. If someone caught sight of the doll before it broke down, the charm lost its force and the person recovered. George Henderson set the account down in his 1911 book Survivals in Belief Among the Celts.
